 Nov 15, 2026 Social Security Isn’t Going Away, but Your Future Benefit Could Be Smaller — 5 Ways To Prepare
 Social Security insolvency may force more Americans to change up their retirement strategy. Written by Heather Altamirano | Edited by Zuri Anderson Add us as a preferred source Warnings that Social Security could be depleted in a few years are making people jittery about retirement, but the truth is, the benefits won’t completely stop. However, the monthly checks could be smaller.
 The program is facing significant financial problems, and the Social Security Board of Trustees estimates that by the fourth quarter of 2032, only 78% of the benefits will be paid out. But planning now could help lessen the impact of an anticipated reduction.
 Learn More: What the Midterm Results Could Mean for Social Security — and What’s Still Uncertain 
 For You: 8 Clever Ways Retirees Are Earning Up to $1K Per Month From Home 
 Finance experts share five ways to prepare for potentially reduced future benefits .
 1. Check Your Social Security Record
 Your Social Security record dates back to your first paying job, and checking it regularly can ensure there are no inaccuracies. Those earnings help determine future benefits, and correcting an error can be more difficult decades later.
 “Everyone should be pulling their Social Security statement once a year,” said Matt Twiford, managing partner of Pegacorn Group LLC . “It shows your earnings record and your projected benefit.”
 Workers can use the statement to see their earnings history and estimated retirement benefit.
 2. Build a Retirement Plan That Works With a Smaller Benefit
 Don't count on Social Security to get you through retirement. Experts are now recommending growing your retirement savings in other ways.
 “The practical move is to not treat the benefit number on your Social Security statement as a promise,” Twiford said. “Build your plan so it works if that number comes in lower, and treat the full amount as upside.”
 That could mean increasing retirement contributions, reassessing your target retirement age or simply running your retirement projections using a lower Social Security benefit.
 3. Consider Both Roth and Traditional Savings
 Roth and traditional savings are smart ways to provide tax diversification. Roth accounts are funded with after-tax dollars, while traditional retirement accounts generally provide a tax benefit up-front and are taxed when money is withdrawn.
 “You pay the tax now at a known rate and withdraw tax-free later at an unknown one,” Twiford said. “Roth only wins if your tax rate in retirement is higher than it is now, and if you're a high earner in your peak years expecting to drop into a lower bracket in retirement, traditional can be the better answer,” he added.
 That's why most people end up wanting both, so they have some control over their taxable income later.
 4. Know What To Focus On at Your Age
 Every generation will be impacted by the reduced benefits, but in different capacities.
 In your 20s and 30s: You have the most time to build retirement savings and tweak your strategy. Twiford said to think about tax rates more than anything. “The national debt is right around $40 trillion, and tax rates today are historically low,” he said, citing Reuters . “Nobody knows what rates look like in 40 years, but the direction of the pressure is not hard to guess.”
 In your 40s and 50s: This age group is the most exposed to the drop in benefits because they’re not young enough to absorb a potential financial hit . Twiford suggested revising your retirement plan in case monthly payments are decreased.
 In your 60s: People in their 60s have the best possible outcome, according to Twiford, because the most serious reform proposals “grandfather current retirees and people close to retirement, because that's the only version that survives politically.”
 With that in mind, Eric Mangold, founder of Argosy Wealth Management , said it’s important to understand the best filing options.
 “The longer you wait to collect your Social Security, the larger it grows, but everyone’s strategy is different,” he said.
 5. Keep Saving
 Whether the hardships with Social Security can be resolved or not isn’t something we can control, but we can put more away for retirement, which is something Mangold recommends.
 “You will need to save more to fill a potential gap,” he said. “Money saved today turns into income in retirement.”
 Social Security's future will depend on decisions about the program, but workers don't have to wait for those decisions before preparing. Checking your earnings record, continuing to save and planning for a potentially smaller benefit can help you build a more resilient retirement strategy.
